item.title: Don’t Pass Your Childhood Traumas Down to Your Kids
item.description:
Trauma

Don’t Pass Your Childhood Traumas Down to Your Kids

How to help break the cycle of dysfunction from one generation to another.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Most of us internalize negative traits from parents and authority figures during our childhoods.
  • When parents react out of their own trauma, they can inadvertently pass the trauma on to their children.
  • Choosing the best course of action, rather than just acting emotionally, often leads to better outcomes.

While growing up, almost all of us on one level or another have inherited some negative traits from our parents and authority figures. Perhaps we have a tendency to be stubborn and dig our heels in when frustrated. Perhaps we lose our tempers and yell at the people closest to us when we become overwhelmed. Maybe we badmouth people when we get angry or even act out physically by throwing things.

It’s an unfortunate fact that many of the traits we disliked in our parents are the same ones we display when we're under stress. These traits don't mean we're bad people, they are things we've internalized during our lives and may resort to when under pressure. Some of the actions we take are counter-productive and may harm us, our families, and our careers.

Passing Down Dysfunction

For example: If you had a father who was quick to anger and said mean, hurtful things to you, it's possible you may have internalized some of that anger and are quick to lash out at people yourself. You may not always lash out in a mean way, but it’s there in the background because it’s how you saw adults dealing with frustration when you were young. The sad truth is that many hurtful situations that occur in families happen because the person who is lashing out was at one time a victim of the same actions. That’s why it’s so important for parents to understand their own triggers and what causes them to become reactive, so they don’t resort to behaviors that are not the choices they want to make.

The difference between reacting and choosing your behavior is a relatively simple distinction. Reactions are powerful emotional responses that can take over and cause you to behave in ways you may later regret. Choices are when you’ve had the time to consider your options and then move forward thoughtfully. When people are in their reactive state, they tend to make snap decisions that often don't resolve the situation and can even make it worse. When reasoned choices are made, people tend to have less regret because they’ve explored a number of options.

Acting on Your Triggers Can Do More Harm Than Good

Making choices that benefit us rather than harm us is in all of our best interests. The problem is that when we become triggered, we often escalate the situation before we're even aware that we're being controlled by our emotions. These triggers can be extremely powerful when activated. This is why we often don't realize we're in a reactive state until we've already done the damage. When we get upset, we often get scared, and, to feel safer, we try to grab control of the situation as quickly and forcefully as possible. We may feel at risk; we may feel we're not heard or respected; or we may feel people are not taking us seriously. This can cause us to react in ways that ultimately come out of our emotions and not our logic.

Often, our feelings of not being heard or respected come from our own childhoods. If you think back to when you were young, you may recall times when a parent or an authority figure lashed out at you because of their frustrations. Perhaps you did something to upset them, or perhaps they were just angry and took it out on you. Either way, this type of lashing out from an adult to a child can cause upset and trauma. The point here is that you don't want to pass that down to your own children.

To avoid doing this, it’s important to understand how overwhelming emotions can be and how they push us toward taking immediate action! Emotions want us to handle the situation right now! We then raise our voices and often make declarations out of anger instead of logic. We escalate situations by raising our voices, trying to grab control, and lashing out in anger. This rarely leads to a positive outcome.

Noticing Emotional Escalation

To try and mitigate this knee-jerk reactiveness, we can work on noticing what happens to us when we start to become escalated emotionally. Are we raising our voice? Are we more interested in making our point than listening? Is winning the argument more important than whether we have a valid point to make? These can be clues to see if we are open to a discussion or just want to win the argument and get our way. The more time we take to consider not only our view, but the view of the person we're talking to, the more likely we will make a reasoned choice rather than just an emotional reaction.

Controlling our reactivity is not easy to put into practice. When our emotions are activated, they think they speak for us and don’t feel they have to consider anything other than what they want at the moment. Unfortunately, when we allow our emotions to run rampant and lash out at others, including our kids, it can lead to hurt feelings and potential trauma that can last for years. As caring parents, we want to set good examples for our children. Being able to recognize our emotional reactivity and not allow it to completely control our actions is one of the best ways to help our kids see there’s a way to listen to our emotions without being controlled by them.

item.title: The Burnout Fix That’s Been Sitting Next to You All Along
item.description:
Burnout

The Burnout Fix That’s Been Sitting Next to You All Along

Who you work with, and how they make you feel, changes how hard work feels.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Social support doesn't erase stress. It changes how the brain reads it, from overwhelmed to capable.
  • Leaders energize teams two ways: with authentic support to each person, and by building bonds across the team.
  • Believing support is available matters as much as receiving it. "I have your back" shifts the landscape.
  • Camaraderie isn't a perk. Teams with real trust find challenges less daunting than going it alone.

Picture two people facing the same brutal Monday: back-to-back meetings, an inbox that never empties, a deadline that keeps moving. One is quietly drowning. The other, somehow, stays afloat. It's the same job and the same pressure. What's different?

Chances are, it's the people around them.

Over the past few decades, a compelling body of research has assembled a striking case: Social connection doesn't just make work more pleasant. It fundamentally changes how difficult and threatening challenges appear to us.

Hills Look Steeper Alone

In a now-famous 2008 study in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, researchers had participants stand at the base of a steep hill wearing a heavy backpack and estimate its steepness. Those who stood alone rated the hill as significantly steeper than those standing beside a friend. The effect grew stronger the longer and warmer the friendship. In a follow-up, participants who merely imagined a supportive person nearby also saw the hill as less steep, while imagining someone they disliked made it look steeper still.

The researchers concluded that the brain treats supportive relationships as a kind of psychological energy. When you feel connected, your nervous system lightens the load. The perception of the challenge changes.

This sits within a much larger body of evidence. Social support shifts how the brain appraises stress, moving us from a threat state (not enough resources to meet the demands) to a challenge state (I can handle this). That shift shows up in lower cortisol, reduced blood pressure, and measurably better performance under pressure.

Enter Relational Energy

Research on relational energy, the feeling of uplift and renewed zest that follows a positive interaction, bridges the social support literature and the daily reality of work. We have all felt it: a conversation that leaves you more motivated than when it started, or a leader who leaves energy in the room rather than draining it.

In my forthcoming book with Kim Cameron, Relational Energy: How to Beat Burnout and Ignite Your Team (Berrett-Koehler, January 2027), we identify a distinctive quality of leaders who are perceived as energizing: They helped their people feel less overwhelmed by stressors. Across the board, the energizing leaders we interviewed demonstrated to their team, consistently and credibly, that they had their back and were committed to their success. That signal — you are not alone in this — transformed how pressure was experienced.

Critically, these leaders knew their own support was only half the equation. We found that they were equally purposeful about fostering camaraderie within the team, cultivating relationships among members, not just between themselves and each individual. Collective support, the sense that the whole group is in it together, was just as powerful a buffer as anything a leader could provide. A team that genuinely has each other's backs perceives the work differently.

This maps onto the hill study mentioned. The hill doesn't shrink, but when someone trustworthy stands beside you and the whole team is behind you, your nervous system reads the situation differently. The demand is the same; the perceived resources are greater. The result is challenge rather than threat.

The Workplace Is Not Exempt

Source: Vectorfusionart / Shutterstock

Burnout is often framed as a workload problem: too many tasks, too little time. Those things matter. But research increasingly points to something running underneath: the erosion of social connection. When people feel isolated and unseen, the same tasks that might feel challenging begin to feel overwhelming. For instance, the email backlog may look like evidence of failure. The workload stops feeling manageable and starts feeling insurmountable.

Lazarus and Folkman's foundational stress and coping theory tells us stress is not simply a property of situations. It results from an appraisal, a judgment about whether our resources measure up to the demands we face. Social support is one of our most powerful resources, and unlike many, it is shaped by the culture and relationships of the places we spend most of our waking hours.

The Leader's Dilemma and Its Answer

Most leaders are caught in a bind. On one side, there's relentless pressure to perform. On the other, there's a team already stretched and at risk of burning out. More pressure feels like it will break people, but easing up feels unaffordable.

Our research and the work of others make it clear: It is not the volume of demands alone that drives burnout. It is facing those demands without perceiving support and compassion from others. Leaders who invest in genuine connection, who make their commitment explicit, who build cultures of mutual support, are changing the psychological conditions under which their team encounters pressure. They are making the hill look smaller, without removing it.

What This Means in Practice

Create supportive connections before they are needed. The protective effect comes largely from perceived availability, the belief that support is there, not just from receiving it in a crisis.

Harness the exponential effect of relational energy so morale doesn't rest on the leader alone. Each positive interaction deposits into a reservoir the team draws on when pressure peaks.

Recognize that camaraderie is a strategy, not a perk. Build connections among team members, not just between yourself and each individual. Mutual trust is the infrastructure that determines how a team weathers difficulty.

Emphasize quality over quantity. The hill studies found that warmth and duration predicted perception more than mere company. A smaller team with genuine trust offers far more protection than a room of polite strangers.

The Antidote Was Relational All Along

We tend to treat burnout as an individual problem requiring individual fixes: better habits, more boundaries, and improved resilience. Our research redirects attention to the quality of our workplace connections — to the leader who conveys "I have your back" and to the team whose members show up for one another and share a genuine sense of camaraderie.

The work won't get easier. But together, the hill looks different.
